<span class=\"quartier-margin-date\" ari: 1984In 1984, a former market-garden hall was turned into a performance venue. It became the Espace Julien — a community centre that would gradually grow into one of the most important contemporary music venues in the south of France. Not through millions spent on architects or grand cultural policies, but through the stubborn determination of people who loved music and sharing it.

2016In 2016, Marseille city council announced an “urban regeneration” project for place Jean-Jaurès. Regeneration — the word is gentle, almost neutral. What it covered was less so: a complete redevelopment of a working-class square, changes to its market, a transformation of how it was used. Some residents immediately saw what that meant in practice: the planned disappearance of what gave the neighbourhood its life, in favour of a cleaner, smoother space, more appealing to a different clientele.

2019In February 2019, the council had a 2.5-metre-high concrete wall put up around the whole square overnight. A staggeringly brutal decision — the kind of gesture that tells you everything about the relationship between an institution and the people it serves once dialogue has broken down. The market was suspended. The square vanished behind the concrete. The neighbourhood lived with that scar for months.

2023In 2023, after 39 years and some 8,000 shows, the Espace Julien changed hands. The association La Responsabilité des Rêves — born from the coming together of Le Makeda, the Théâtre de l’Œuvre, La Meson and the Espace Julien — took over the keys. The venue reopened on 22 September, with a new look and the same ambition. The story goes on.

2024In 2024, Éditions Parenthèses published Espace Julien, une aventure musicale à Marseille (Patrick Coulomb, Marie-Hélène Balivet), a book that traces those four decades through stage photos, posters and artists’ accounts. A fine book about an unlikely place that changed a city’s cultural life.

Côté musique, c’est un pub rock et métal: Musically, it is a rock and metal pub: gigs range from blues to “seriously angry” metal, by way of rock’n’roll. Around a hundred people, a small stage, a small terrace. The kind of place where you come in for a beer and stay for the band.
C’est ce qui fait le charme de l’endroit: That is what makes the place special: here, musicians host other musicians, and their audience, in the space where they rehearse every day. Rehearsal rooms, a recording studio, a small gig room: the nights are often unusual, and that is exactly why people go.
C’est de la grignote efficace, pas chère: It’s snacking done right: quick, cheap and excellent. You eat under the Maradona posters with a glass of Malbec, and you’re not the only fans: Balerdi, Rulli and Medina used to eat here before leaving OM this summer.
C’est excellent et bien garni, à petits: It’s excellent and generously filled, at small prices. After a Koujina sandwich, the snack quest can call it a day.
C’est gourmand, et l’équipe est super sy: It’s indulgent, and the team are lovely: you dither for ages, they help you choose, you leave with two. It’s the only stop on the quest where you can start with dessert.
C’est ici que la densité est la plus for: This is where the density is highest. On Rue Pastoret, murals cover the façades from top to bottom: huge black-and-white portraits, lettering, comic-book characters. Shop windows are painted right up to the signs.
C’est la gentrification : un processus s: This is gentrification: a slow, structural process with no clearly identifiable villain, and yet a very real social violence. Cours Julien is no exception. For Marseille, it is even one of its most visible symbols.
C’est la plus belle façon d’arriver. Par: It is the best way to arrive. Via Cours Lieutaud and the Rue Armand-Bédarride steps, built around 1864 and covered in graffiti, or via the streets climbing up to Cours Julien, you discover the neighbourhood the way it was built: on a slope, in steps, in painted walls.
C’est l’adresse neuve de la liste, ou pr: This is the newest address on the list, or almost. The Café Julien, the Espace Julien’s small venue, reopened on 2 October 2026 after several months of work. By merging with the building’s main hall, its capacity has gone from 180 to 280. A large window now opens it onto cours Julien, the acoustics have been redone, and the bar is wheelchair accessible.
C’est l’adresse pour manger au calme, av: It’s the place to eat in peace, alone with your thoughts, a little away from the bustle of La Plaine. Open Tuesday to Sunday, lunch and dinner.
C’est l’image que tout le monde vient ch: This is the picture everyone comes for. The great staircase links Cours Julien to the streets at the bottom of the neighbourhood, and not a centimetre of bare stone is left: steps, railings, walls, lamp posts, everything is painted. The layers have been building up for years, so the staircase never looks the same twice.

Depuis trente ans, l’Espace Julien fait: For thirty years, the Espace Julien has kept the cours beating to the rhythm of live music. It is the neighbourhood’s big hall: 990 standing, 600 seated, artists from all over the world and Marseille bands playing their biggest show. And yet the venue insists: “Here, artists and audience are close together.”
Depuis un an, la grignote a changé d’éch: Over the past year, snacking here has gone up a gear. On Rue Pastoret, within fifty metres, you go from Vietnam to Apulia. The empanadas come from Buenos Aires, the durums from the Levant, the kafteji from Tunis, the royal sandwich from Pakistan. To make sense of it all, we’ve put everything in a vending machine, sorted by shape: folded, rolled, cut in half, for sharing. Sixteen slots, nearly all of them cheap. Each time you try one, stamp your ticket: the snack quest begins.

La place Jean-Jaurès — que tout le monde: Place Jean-Jaurès — which everyone calls “La Plaine” — was for a long time the beating heart of the working-class neighbourhood. A market three times a week, café terraces spreading across the tarmac, old men playing pétanque, kids hanging around. An old-style square, functional, worn, alive precisely because it was not pretty.
La place a rouvert. Les travaux sont fin: The square has reopened. The works are finished. The market is back, but not quite the same. New terraces, new street furniture, a resurfaced ground. Some say it is better. Others say something is missing — that roughness, that discomfort, that freedom of use which meant the square belonged to everyone because it was not pretty for anyone in particular.

Le Cours Julien tire son nom d’un ancien: Cours Julien takes its name from a former market garden that stretched across what is now the esplanade. Perhaps that is why it has kept its particular texture — streets that do not always meet at right angles, buildings that seem to have been set down almost by chance, cellars that become music venues.

À Marseille, les murs parlent fort, et n: In Marseille, the walls speak loudly, and nowhere more than in Cours Julien. Since the 1980s, the neighbourhood has been a canvas for generations of graffiti artists. The works don’t last: they get painted over, answer each other, disappear. That is what makes it the city’s finest open-air gallery.
À côté des verres, une cuisine libanaise: Alongside the drinks comes Lebanese food on small plates, to share as the evening goes on: hummus, grilled cauliflower, falafel, za’atar buns, shawarma. That is the whole idea of the place: welcoming guests the way you would at home, the Lebanese way.
